_comment: The array the ray tracer was run on, in full, so the case can be rebuilt rather than believed.
Frame: +Y is up, +X is east, -Z is north. A panel's azimuth is a compass bearing, 0 = north,
90 = east, 180 = south. Lengths are metres, angles are degrees.
21 columns x 3 rows. The columns sit edge to edge with no gap, so a row approximates the
infinitely long row the closed form assumes; the comparison is taken on the CENTRE panel of the
MIDDLE row, which is the panel furthest from every edge and therefore the one where that
approximation is best. Three rows rather than two so that the measured panel has a row behind it
as well as in front, matching an interior row of a real array.
The panel is 1.6 m along the row axis and 1.0 m up the slope. The slope length is what the
shading fraction is measured against, so keeping it at exactly 1.0 makes the fraction and the
shaded length the same number and removes one place to make an arithmetic slip.

panel.thickness_note: The product builds panels as solid boxes. The closed form assumes zero thickness, and this 4 cm is the single largest reason the two disagree. scene/engine-vs-closed-form.csv also carries a 0.0004 m run, which isolates the sampling error from the thickness.

layout.measured_panel: row index 1 (the middle row), column index 10 (the centre column)

sun_positions._comment: Sun directions are set directly rather than derived from a date and a site, so the case has no dependency on an ephemeris and no timezone to get wrong. A direction at elevation a and compass azimuth g is (cos a sin g, sin a, -cos a cos g).

quality._comment: Sub-samples per axis across the panel face. The product clamps this to 7; the higher counts are here only to show that the disagreement converges to zero, which is what tells a quadrature error apart from a modelling error.
